summary:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is an open-access, public web tool created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to visualize how our infrared universe evolves across repeated sky passes. Designed for students, citizen scientists, and astronomers, it turns complex spectroscopic data from NASA’s SPHEREx mission into an intuitive, interactive time-series viewer.

Built with FastAPI and responsive vanilla web standards, the tool connects directly to the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) TAP service and Simbad/NED resolvers. Users can search celestial targets (like Messier 101) or sky coordinates across SPHEREx’s six detector bands (0.75–5.0 μm). The application features an interactive multi-epoch time slider and an astronomical "Blink Compare" mode to easily spot transient phenomena, asteroids, and variable stars.

To guarantee reliable public access without requiring API keys or heavy scientific software, the pipeline processes multi-extension FITS arrays on the fly using ZScale contrast stretching and wavelength calibration, paired with a bundled 356-epoch verified dataset for instantaneous fallback when archive proxies are busy. Completely responsive, mobile-ready, and keyboard-accessible, the project makes NASA’s deep infrared sky accessible to anyone, anywhere.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a public web-based visualizer designed to explore how the infrared universe changes over time across repeated sky surveys.

  • Target Resolution & Search: Users enter a celestial object name (like M101 or Vega) or specific celestial coordinates (Right Ascension / Declination) and choose one of SPHEREx’s six detector bands (0.75–5.0 μm). The backend resolves targets via CDS Simbad/NED and executes Table Access Protocol (TAP) queries against the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).
  • FITS Data Processing: Raw multi-extension FITS data is ingested, calibrated for wavelength (WCS-WAVE), and processed using astronomical contrast stretching (ZScale and Asinh) to reveal faint celestial objects without blowing out bright cores.
  • Interactive Visualization: The web viewer displays observations in chronological order. Users can scrub through time using an interactive slider, play back temporal image sequences, or activate the "Blink Compare" mode (alternating between two chosen epochs at 2 Hz or 4 Hz) to spot moving asteroids, variable stars, and transient events.
  • Fail-Safe Fallback: If upstream NASA TAP archive servers are busy or timing out, the system automatically switches to a verified 356-epoch bundled dataset so the user experience is never interrupted.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Zero Barrier to Entry: Requires no software installation (like DS9), no API keys, and no Python environment. Anyone with a smartphone or laptop browser can view and inspect NASA mission data.
  • Scientific Accuracy: Uses genuine astronomical algorithms (ZScale, Asinh, WCS coordinate transformations, and exact spectral wavelengths) rather than generic graphic filters.
  • Instant Temporal Comparison: Finding transient objects or moving asteroids manually across static tables is tedious; the automated Blink Comparator and time-series slider allow the human eye to detect subtle changes in seconds.
  • High Availability & Resilience: With client-side image caching and automatic fallback to verified local datasets, the tool remains functional even during upstream NASA server maintenance.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Democratizing Space Science: SPHEREx is mapping millions of galaxies and stellar environments; this tool makes that data accessible to educators, high school/university students, and amateur astronomers worldwide.
  • Citizen Science & Asteroid Hunting: Enables citizen scientists to visually inspect repeated sky passes to help identify transients, supernovae, asteroid tracks, and variable stars that might otherwise stay buried in database rows.
  • Public Engagement: Fosters global curiosity and appreciation for NASA’s astrophysics missions through an intuitive, interactive interface.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Programming Languages: Python 3.11+ (Backend) and Vanilla JavaScript ES2022+, HTML5, CSS3 (Frontend).
    • Backend: FastAPI (asynchronous REST API), Uvicorn (ASGI web server), Astropy (FITS parsing, WCS coordinates, ZScale/Asinh stretching), Astroquery (NASA IRSA TAP & Simbad/NED queries), NumPy, and Pillow (PIL).
    • Frontend: Modern Vanilla Web APIs (AbortController, fetch, HTML5 Canvas/Image elements) without bloated third-party frameworks.
  • Testing & Quality Assurance: Pytest test suite (19 unit/integration tests) verifying coordinate conversions, FITS stretching, API error handling, and mock TAP queries.
  • Hosting & DevOps: Render (Docker containerized cloud deployment), GitHub (version control and CI/CD).
  • Hardware: Standard consumer desktop/laptop computers running Windows and Linux environments.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Modernizing the Classical "Blink Comparator": The project pays homage to Clyde Tombaugh’s 1930 manual optical blink comparator (used to discover Pluto) by modernizing it into a responsive, touch-friendly, web-based digital blink engine running directly on modern infrared data.
  • Pixel-Accurate Scientific Display: Rather than smoothing or interpolating pixels, the viewer applies CSS image-rendering: pixelated, preserving raw detector pixel boundaries so users see true scientific data rather than artificial rendering artifacts.
  • Graceful Degradation Architecture: Instead of breaking or throwing technical error pop-ups when scientific archives experience high traffic, the app uses an intelligent tiered fallback mechanism that transitions cleanly into verified mission data with transparent user notifications.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Universal Accessibility (a11y): Full keyboard shortcuts (Space to toggle playback, ←/→ for frames, B for blink comparison), ARIA live regions for screen readers, high-contrast dark theme, and focus indicators.
  • Mobile & Cross-Device Responsiveness: Touch-friendly slider controls and responsive CSS layout optimized for everything from a 390px mobile viewport to widescreen monitors.
  • Performance & Bandwidth Optimization: Asynchronous progressive loading and in-memory image caching ensure that only necessary frames are fetched, saving user mobile data and minimizing server load.
  • NASA Space Apps Guidelines: Ensuring open-source transparency (MIT License), full attribution of NASA/IPAC data sources, and strict adherence to open science principles.
